extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, inventors, USPTO staff, policymakers, and congressional staff
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and explanation of provisions in the Patent Reform Act (America Invents Act) concerning priority rules, prior art/grace period, post‑grant proceedings, PTO authority, fees, and procedural safeguards. Useful for practitioners evaluating how the bill changes patentability and administrative-review processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual independent audit of the Office
rubrics_metrics.description: (f) Audit.--The Under Secretary shall, on an annual basis, provide for an independent audit of the financial statements of the Office. Such audit shall be conducted in accordance with generally acceptable accounting procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires the Under Secretary to arrange an annual independent audit of the Office's financial statements, conducted per generally acceptable accounting procedures (GAAP). No scoring guidance; procedural/oversight requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund to submit business-type budget to President
rubrics_metrics.description: (g) Budget.--The Fund shall prepare and submit each year to the President a business-type budget in a manner, and before a date, as the President prescribes by regulation for the budget program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandates annual preparation and submission of a business‑type budget by the Fund to the President, according to President-prescribed form/timing. Procedural requirement for budgetary planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budgetary effects determined by PAYGO statement
rubrics_metrics.description: The budgetary effects of this Act, for the purpose of complying with the Statutory Pay-As-You-Go-Act of 2010, shall be determined by reference to the latest statement titled 'Budgetary Effects of PAYGO Legislation' for this Act, submitted for printing in the Congressional Record by the Chairman of the Senate Budget Committee, provided that such statement has been submitted prior to the vote on passage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes how PAYGO compliance is to be measured for the Act—by reference to the most recent PAYGO statement submitted before the vote. Procedural for legislative scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: First‑inventor‑to‑file priority rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the first-to-file system... priority is determined by when the application for patent was filed. Whichever inventor files first has priority, and third-party prior art is measured against the filing date, and is invalidating if it disclosed the invention before the date when the application was filed, rather than the date when the invention was conceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replaces first‑to‑invent priority (based on conception/proof) with an objective filing‑date rule; emphasis on filing promptly (including provisional filings) to secure priority. Practical implications and contrasts with interference practice are discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sec. 102 — Conditions for patentability; novelty/prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Sec. 102. CONDITIONS FOR PATENTABILITY; NOVELTY(a) Novelty; Prior Art.--A person shall be entitled to a patent unless--(1) the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date of the claimed invention; or(2) the claimed invention was described in a patent issued under section 151, or in an application for patent published or deemed published under section 122(b), in which the patent or application, as the case may be, names another inventor and was effectively filed before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines what counts as statutory prior art against a claimed invention (measured against the effective filing date). Use filing-date analysis to assess novelty; includes patents, publications, public use, on-sale, or other public availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: 102(b) Exceptions — one‑year grace period for inventor disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: (b) Exceptions.-- (1) Disclosures made 1 year or less before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.--A disclosure made 1 year or less before the effective filing date of a claimed invention shall not be prior art to the claimed invention under subsection (a)(1) if--(A) the disclosure was made by the inventor or joint inventor or by another who obtained the subject matter disclosed directly or indirectly from the inventor or a joint inventor; or(B) the subject matter disclosed had, before such disclosure, been publicly disclosed by the inventor or a joint inventor or another who obtained the subject matter disclosed directly or indirectly from the inventor or a joint inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creates a one‑year exception (grace period) protecting inventor-originated disclosures (and disclosures by those who obtained the invention from the inventor) made within one year before the effective filing date. Clarifies that such disclosures will not be treated as prior art under 102(a)(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: 'First to publish' protection for inventor disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor who publishes his invention, or discloses it at a trade show or academic conference, or otherwise makes it publicly available, has an absolute right to priority if he files an application within one year of his disclosure. No application effectively filed after his disclosure, and no prior art disclosed after his disclosure, can defeat his application for patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains practical protection afforded to inventors who publicly disclose: public disclosure by the inventor grants a one‑year safe harbor against later third‑party disclosures, so filing within that year preserves patent rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional application as practical priority tool
rubrics_metrics.description: A provisional application requires only a written description of the invention and how to make it. Once a provisional application is filed, the inventor has a year to file a completed application. Currently, filing a provisional application costs $220 for a large entity, and $110 for a small entity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages use of provisional applications to secure a filing date cheaply and buy time to prepare full applications—positioned as a realistic alternative to relying on first‑to‑invent proof (invention notebooks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher thresholds for instituting inter partes and post‑grant review
rubrics_metrics.description: The present bill imposes higher thresholds, requiring a reasonable likelihood of invalidity for inter partes review, and more‑likely‑than‑not invalidity for post‑grant review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raised institution thresholds are intended to weed out marginal challenges, preserve PTO resources, and force petitioners to front‑load their cases so proceedings can be resolved more quickly. This is a quality/resource‑management criterion for post‑grant processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter partes review to be conducted as adjudicative proceeding (burden on challenger)
rubrics_metrics.description: The present bill makes this change, repealing requirements that inter partes be run on an examinational model and allowing the PTO to adopt an adjudicative model, where the burden of proof is on the challenger and the office simply decides whether the challenger has met his burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shifts inter partes from examiner‑style reexamination to an adjudicative model with challenger bearing proof burden; intended to alter procedure and evidentiary expectations in administrative review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on serial administrative challenges and coordination with litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: The present bill does coordinate inter partes and post‑grant review with litigation, barring use of these proceedings if the challenger seeks a declaratory judgment that a patent is invalid, and setting a time limit for seeking inter partes review if the petitioner or related parties is sued for infringement of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aims to reduce duplicative/serial attacks on patents and to coordinate timing between litigation and administrative proceedings so as to prevent strategic/serial use of multiple administrative avenues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on third‑party ex parte reexamination (administrative estoppel)
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill’s enhanced administrative estoppel will effectively bar a third party or related parties from invoking ex parte reexamination against a patent if that third party has already employed post‑grant or inter partes review against that patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents parties from using ex parte reexamination to re‑litigate issues already addressed in other administrative proceedings by the same or related parties; reduces serial challenges and preserves estoppel consequences from prior administrative filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO may reject requests presenting same or substantially same art/arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Also, the bill allows the Patent Office to reject any request for a proceeding, including a request for ex parte reexamination, if the same or substantially the same prior art or arguments previously were presented to the Office with respect to that patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives the PTO discretionary authority to refuse proceedings that would rehash previously presented art/arguments, further limiting repetitious administrative attacks and conserving PTO resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO ramp‑up period and ability to delay implementation of new proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Among other things, the present bill authorizes a ramp‑up period, allowing the office to limit the number of proceedings that can be implemented during the first 4 years after the new proceeding becomes effective. The present bill includes a number of safeguards... the present bill includes the PTO be allowed to delay implementation of post‑grant review if the office lacks the resources to implement that new proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Safeguard to ensure PTO has capacity to administer new post‑grant proceedings: limits initial caseload and permits postponement if resources are insufficient, to avoid overburdening the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of treble damages for willful infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The present bill does so, eliminating the restrictive three‑buckets approach and broad safe harbors that appeared in the bill in 2009. The report also recommended that the bill remove subjective elements from patent law... The present bill effectively makes both changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintains meaningful damages deterrent for willful/calcified infringement by preserving treble damages and removing prior statutory safe harbors that would have limited such relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of subjective intent elements and patent‑forfeiture doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: The report also recommended that the bill remove subjective elements from patent law, such as the various deceptive‑intent elements throughout the code and the patent‑forfeiture doctrines. The present bill effectively makes both changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removes subjective/deceptive‑intent based penalties and antiquated forfeiture rules to make patent law more objective, predictable, and less dependent on intent-based factfinding.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO fee setting authority and ending fee diversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Fee setting authority is present in S. 23 (see Section 9) and Senator Tom Coburn plans to introduce an Amendment that would once and for all eliminate fee diversion and let the USPTO keep the fees it collects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives USPTO the ability to set and retain fees to reinvest in operations and reduce backlog; policy intended to enable agency resource self‑sufficiency and modernization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition/interpretation of 'disclosure' and 'publicly accessible' for prior art/grace period
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure is something that makes the invention available to the public--the same test applied by section 102(a) to define the scope of relevant prior art. And 'available to the public' means the same thing that 'publicly accessible' does in the context of a publication. Subject matter makes an invention publicly accessible or available if an interested person who is skilled in the field could, through reasonable diligence, find the subject matter and understand the invention from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides interpretive guidance to determine whether an activity constitutes a disclosure for 102(a) and thus whether the 102(b) grace period applies; aligns 'disclosure' with the statutory prior‑art accessibility standard so the grace period is not narrower than prior‑art scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear, objective rules for prior art and priority dates
rubrics_metrics.description: These rules are highly protective of inventors... These rules are also clear, objective, and transparent. They create unambiguous guidelines for inventors. To figure out if a patent is valid against prior art, all that a manufacturer needs to do is look at the patent’s filing date and figure out whether the inventor publicly disclosed the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes predictability: validity can be assessed by checking filing dates and inventor disclosures rather than subjective inquiries. Intended to simplify prior‑art searches and reduce uncertainty for practitioners and industry.
